questions.q: According to the lesson, why does research code need version control just as much as production software?
options: Without it, the honest answer to 'what did the code look like when it produced this result?' is usually 'I don't know,' which git's dated, ordered history solves directly
Because research code is legally required to use git in most institutions
Because git automatically fixes numerical bugs in simulation code
Because notebooks cannot be saved without git installed
questions.explain: The lesson's core argument is that answering 'which code version produced this number?' reliably requires a real history, which naming files 'final_FINAL_v2.py' can never provide as well as git log can.

questions.q: What makes the commit message 'Fix sign error in CNOT control-qubit projector...' (with an explanation of the bug) more useful for research code than 'fix bug'?
options: It is shorter and therefore easier for git to store
Git requires commit messages to be at least three lines long
There is no real difference; message content doesn't matter for research code
It tells a future reader what was wrong and why the new version's numeric output can now be trusted, not just that something changed
questions.explain: For numerical code, a commit message that explains *why* a change was made -- especially when it affects a result -- lets a future reader understand what changed and why the new output is trustworthy, which 'fix bug' doesn't convey at all.

questions.q: What does a git tag like `v1.0-bell-fidelity-result` let you do that a regular commit on the main branch does not guarantee?
options: Reliably find and restore the exact code state behind a specific published number, even after many later commits change `main`
Automatically recompute the fidelity value if the code changes
Prevent anyone from ever modifying the gates.py file again
Tags are identical to commits in every respect and provide no additional guarantee
questions.explain: A tag is a permanent named marker on one specific commit, so `git checkout` on that tag always reconstructs that exact code state regardless of how far `main` has since moved -- which an ordinary commit reference doesn't promise as a stable, memorable anchor.

questions.q: Per the lesson's `.gitignore` guidance, why do large raw simulated shot-data files generally NOT belong in version control, while a small final result file (e.g. the 0.9987 fidelity value as JSON) does?
options: Large regeneratable data bloats repository history without adding information beyond what the code plus its seed can reproduce, while the small final number is exactly the specific claim worth keeping and checking against
Raw shot data should never be saved anywhere, including outside of git
Git technically cannot store any file larger than a few kilobytes
Small files are always excluded from git by default, and large files are always included
questions.explain: The distinguishing factor is regeneratability plus size: large raw output can be regenerated from the code and seed and just bloats history, while a small specific result is worth version-controlling precisely because it's the claim other commits get checked against.

questions.q: If fixing a real bug changes a previously published numeric result, what does the lesson identify as the actual problem to avoid?
options: Using git tags at all, since they make old results too easy to find
Silently overwriting the old number with no trace or explanation, rather than the fact that a legitimate bug fix changed the result
The fact that any bug fix ever changes a number, which should never be allowed to happen
Writing a commit message that explains the bug fix
questions.explain: The lesson frames the bug fix itself, and the resulting changed number, as expected and fine -- the actual failure would be hiding the change instead of documenting what was wrong and updating anyone relying on the old number.
